claim: Head-fixed mice learn to anticipate reward during appetitive auditory trace conditioning (AATC).
source: Head-fixed mice learn to anticipate reward during AATC
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data showing emergence of anticipatory licking in response to CS+ sounds.

claim: Mice were trained to associate one of two sounds (CS+ vs CS−) with a liquid reward delivered after a 1-s-long, silent trace period.
source: We trained head-fixed mice to associate one of two sounds (CS+ vs CS−) with a liquid reward delivered after a 1-s-long, silent trace period (Figure 1A; Otis et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and cites a previous study using similar methodology.

claim: Successful learning expressed as the emergence of anticipatory licking of the animals in response to CS+ sounds.
source: Successful learning expressed as the emergence of anticipatory licking of the animals in response to CS+ sounds (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in figures and described in text.

claim: Across all animals, lick rates during the trace period were significantly higher during CS+ trials after 5 days of training.
source: Across all animals, lick rates during the trace period were significantly higher during CS+ trials after 5 days of training (Figure 1C; Wilcoxon rank sum, p < 0.01).
evidence: Statistical test results support this claim with p < 0.01.

claim: High-density silicon probe recordings were performed from the hippocampal CA1 area and the prefrontal cortex (PFC) in mice.
source: we employed high-density electrophysiological recordings from the hippocampal CA1 area and the prefrontal cortex (PFC) in mice
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: 1636 cells were recorded in total from CA1 with an average of 34 cells per session.
source: 1636 and 2217 cells total and 34 and 54 average per session in CA1 and PFC, respectively
evidence: This provides quantitative data about the number of recorded neurons.

claim: 2217 cells were recorded in total from PFC with an average of 54 cells per session.
source: 1636 and 2217 cells total and 34 and 54 average per session in CA1 and PFC, respectively
evidence: This provides quantitative data about the number of recorded neurons.

claim: Short-latency evoked responses to both CS+ and CS− stimuli increased over the course of learning in CA1.
source: Short-latency evoked responses to both CS+ and CS− stimuli increased over the course of learning in CA1 (Kruskal–Wallis test; F(3,3267) = 23.64, p < 0.001; post hoc Wilcoxon rank sum test for CS+, p < 0.001 and CS−, p = 0.008)
evidence: Statistical tests support this claim with p < 0.001 for overall effect and specific post-hoc comparisons.

claim: In CA1, CS+ and CS− responses were not significantly different from each other postlearning.
source: but were not significantly different from each other postlearning (Figure 1G, Wilcoxon rank sum, p = 0.73)
evidence: Statistical test shows no significant difference with p = 0.73.

claim: In PFC, CS+ responses remained high during learning but responses to CS− stimuli decreased.
source: In contrast, in PFC, CS+ responses remained high during learning but responses to CS− stimuli decreased (Kruskal–Wallis test; F(3,4413) = 21.49, p < 0.001; post hoc Wilcoxon rank sum test for CS+, p = 0.2 and CS−, p < 0.001)
evidence: Statistical tests support this claim with significant overall effect and specific post-hoc comparisons.

claim: In PFC, postlearning responses between CS+ and CS− stimuli were significantly different.
source: which led to significant differences in postlearning responses between CS+ and CS− stimuli (Figure 1L, Wilcoxon rank sum p < 0.05)
evidence: Statistical test supports this with p < 0.05.

claim: During the trace period following CS+ sounds, cells in PFC exhibited, on average, a strong sustained increase in firing rates.
source: During the trace period following CS+ sounds, cells in PFC exhibited, on average, a strong sustained increase in firing rates (Wilcoxon rank sum, p < 0.001) (Figure 1M)
evidence: Statistical test supports this with p < 0.001.

claim: During the trace period, average single-cell responses in CA1 became significantly suppressed.
source: while average single-cell responses in CA1 became significantly suppressed (Wilcoxon rank sum, p < 0.001) (Figure 1H)
evidence: Statistical test supports this with p < 0.001.

claim: Reward evoked activity significantly decreased in both CA1 and PFC from pre- to postlearning sessions.
source: Reward evoked activity significantly decreased in both CA1 (Wilcoxon rank sum, p < 0.001) and PFC (Wilcoxon rank sum, p < 0.001) (Figure 1I and N) from pre- to postlearning sessions.
evidence: Statistical tests support this for both brain regions with p < 0.001.

claim: Single cells in PFC showed increases in activity at the time of the first anticipatory lick (PFC Lick-Up, n = 77, 4% of all cells).
source: we found that single cells in PFC showed increases in activity compared to pretrial baseline at the time of the first anticipatory lick (PFC Lick-Up, n = 77, 4% of all cells; criterion: mean activity during −250 to +250 ms around first lick, one standard deviation above pretrial baseline) (Figure 2D)
evidence: Quantitative data and criteria for classification are provided.

claim: A small population of CA1 cells responded during licking (CA1 Lick-Up, n = 36, 2%).
source: We also found that a small population of CA1 cells responded during licking (CA1 Lick-Up, n = 36, 2%) (Figure 2A)
evidence: Quantitative data about the number and percentage of lick-responsive cells is provided.

claim: In CA1, a large fraction of nonlick cells was significantly suppressed by CS+ stimuli (post Trace-Down, n = 580, 40%).
source: In CA1, a large fraction of nonlick cells was significantly suppressed by CS+ stimuli (post Trace-Down, n = 580, 40%) (Figure 2B and C, bottom)
evidence: Quantitative data about the number and percentage of suppressed cells is provided.

claim: The percentage of Trace-Down cells in CA1 increased from pre- to postlearning (Pre 19%).
source: and the percentage of these Trace-Down cells as well as suppression levels increased from pre- to postlearning (Pre 19 %; Suppression Pre vs Post, t-test, p < 0.01)
evidence: Statistical test supports this with p < 0.01.

claim: In CA1, a smaller fraction of nonlick cells showed sustained increases to CS+ sounds (post Trace-Up, n = 247, 17%).
source: We also observed a smaller fraction of nonlick cells with sustained increases to CS+ sounds (post Trace-Up, n = 247, 17%) (Figure 2B and C, bottom)
evidence: Quantitative data about the number and percentage of activated cells is provided.

claim: The percentages of Trace-Up cells in CA1 decreased from pre- to postlearning session (Pre, 29%).
source: The percentages of these cells decreased from pre- to postlearning session (Pre, 29%, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B)
evidence: Quantitative data comparing pre- and postlearning percentages is provided.

claim: In PFC, most modulated cells showed sustained increases in activity in response to CS+ sounds (Trace-Up, n = 734, 38%).
source: In PFC, most modulated cells showed sustained increases in activity in response to CS+ sounds (Trace-Up, n = 734, 38%) (Figure 2E and F, top)
evidence: Quantitative data about the number and percentage of activated cells is provided.

claim: In PFC, the percentage and activation levels of Trace-Up cells remained similar from pre- to postlearning.
source: and the percentage and activation levels of these cells remained similar from pre- to postlearning
evidence: This describes the stability of Trace-Up cell properties across learning.

claim: In PFC, a similar fraction of cells showed sustained suppression (Trace-Down, n = 630, 33%).
source: A similar fraction of cells showed sustained suppression (Trace-Down, n = 630, 33%) (Figure 2E and F, bottom)
evidence: Quantitative data about the number and percentage of suppressed cells is provided.

claim: CS− responsive Trace-Up cells in PFC significantly decreased their activity from pre- to postlearning sessions.
source: CS− responsive Trace-Up cells in PFC significantly decreased their activity from pre- to postlearning sessions (t-test, p < 0.001) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B)
evidence: Statistical test supports this with p < 0.001.

claim: In postlearning sessions, the population rate vector distance increased after stimulus onset and persists to be significantly different from baseline during the trace period in CA1.
source: We found that in postlearning sessions, the population rate vector distance increased after stimulus onset and persists to be significantly different from baseline during the trace period in CA1 (Wilcoxon sign rank, p < 0.001)
evidence: Statistical test supports this with p < 0.001.

claim: In postlearning sessions, the population rate vector distance increased after stimulus onset and persists to be significantly different from baseline during the trace period in PFC.
source: and PFC (Wilcoxon sign rank, p < 0.001)
evidence: Statistical test supports this with p < 0.001.

claim: Nonlick cell population rate vector distance did not correlate with lick activity in CA1.
source: Nonlick cell population rate vector distance did not correlate with lick activity or movement of the animals in CA1 (n = 36, Population Vector Distance vs Licks: correlation coefficient = 0.14, p = 0.42; Population Vector Distance vs movement: correlation coefficient = 0.03, p = 0.85; Figure 3—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: Correlation analysis shows no significant relationship with p = 0.42.

claim: Nonlick cell population rate vector distance did not correlate with movement of the animals in CA1.
source: Nonlick cell population rate vector distance did not correlate with lick activity or movement of the animals in CA1 (n = 36, Population Vector Distance vs Licks: correlation coefficient = 0.14, p = 0.42; Population Vector Distance vs movement: correlation coefficient = 0.03, p = 0.85; Figure 3—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: Correlation analysis shows no significant relationship with p = 0.85.

claim: Nonlick cell population rate vector distance did not correlate with lick activity in PFC.
source: or PFC (n = 38, Population Vector Distance vs Licks: correlation coefficient = −0.1, p = 0.52; Population Vector Distance vs movement: correlation coefficient = –0.04, p = 0.74; Figure 3—figure supplement 2D)
evidence: Correlation analysis shows no significant relationship with p = 0.52.

claim: Nonlick cell population rate vector distance did not correlate with movement of the animals in PFC.
source: or PFC (n = 38, Population Vector Distance vs Licks: correlation coefficient = −0.1, p = 0.52; Population Vector Distance vs movement: correlation coefficient = –0.04, p = 0.74; Figure 3—figure supplement 2D)
evidence: Correlation analysis shows no significant relationship with p = 0.74.

claim: Trial identity could be predicted significantly above chance level in CA1 using trace period firing rates (mean performance, 62% correct).
source: We were able to predict the preceding stimulus identity significantly above chance level in CA1 (mean performance, 62 % correct, Wilcoxon sign rank p < 0.001; Figure 3C)
evidence: Statistical test supports above-chance classification with p < 0.001.

claim: Trial identity could be predicted significantly above chance level in PFC using trace period firing rates (mean performance, 76% correct).
source: and PFC (mean performance, 76 % correct, Wilcoxon sign rank p < 0.001; Figure 3F)
evidence: Statistical test supports above-chance classification with p < 0.001.

claim: CA1 and PFC are known to interact during various spatial memory tasks in rodents.
source: CA1 and PFC are known to interact during various spatial memory tasks in rodents (Benchenane et al., 2010; Jones and Wilson, 2005; Sigurdsson et al., 2010; Spellman et al., 2015)
evidence: Multiple citations support this established finding.

claim: Aversive trace conditioning affects local field potential synchronization within and across brain areas.
source: and aversive trace conditioning affects local field potential synchronization within and across brain areas (Shearkhani and Takehara-Nishiuchi, 2013; Takehara-Nishiuchi et al., 2011)
evidence: Citations support this finding from previous studies.

claim: Postlearning, high-frequency CA1–PFC LFP coherence was increased during CS presentation (60–140 Hz).
source: We found that postlearning, high-frequency CA1–PFC LFP coherence was increased during CS presentation (n = 13, 60–140 Hz permutation test at each frequency <0.05) (Figure 4B)
evidence: Permutation test supports this with p < 0.05 across the frequency range.

claim: During CS+ trials, trace period coherence was significantly elevated across a broad frequency range (12–140 Hz).
source: During CS+ trials, trace period coherence was furthermore significantly elevated across a broad frequency range (n = 13, 12–140 Hz permutation test at each frequency <0.05)
evidence: Permutation test supports this with p < 0.05 across the frequency range.

claim: Postlearning CA1 ensemble activity at baseline could be used to predict other individual neurons firing rates in CA1 just as well as the firing rates of neurons in PFC.
source: We observed that postlearning CA1 ensemble activity at baseline could be used to predict other individual neurons firing rates in CA1 just as well as the firing rates of neurons in PFC
evidence: This is based on reduced-rank regression analysis results.

claim: The PFC ensemble was much better at predicting the firing rates of other PFC neurons compared to neurons in CA1.
source: The PFC ensemble, on the other hand, was much better at predicting the firing rates of other PFC neurons compared to neurons in CA1 (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is based on reduced-rank regression analysis results.

claim: Crossarea predictability of firing rates did not change significantly when comparing baseline levels to any of the different trial stages (Stim, Trace, or Reward).
source: However, crossarea predictability of firing rates did not change significantly when we compared baseline levels to any of the different trial stages (Stim, Trace, or Reward) (Figure 4C, Wilcoxon rank sum test; p < 0.05)
evidence: Statistical test shows no significant differences with p < 0.05 threshold.

claim: In CA1, ensemble activity substantially decorrelated over the course of learning.
source: However, by focusing on CA1, we found that ensemble activity substantially decorrelated over the course of learning
evidence: This is based on reduced-rank regression analysis results.

claim: In CA1, individual cells firing rates were significantly less well predicted by the rest of the ensemble from pre- to postlearning sessions.
source: and individual cells firing rates were significantly less well predicted by the rest of the ensemble from pre- to postlearning sessions
evidence: This is based on reduced-rank regression analysis results.

claim: In PFC, ensemble activity did not decorrelate over the course of learning.
source: This was not the case in PFC (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is based on reduced-rank regression analysis results showing no change.

claim: Reactivation of task-related assemblies in PFC increases significantly over the course of learning during hippocampal aSWRs.
source: We found that reactivation of task-related assemblies in PFC increases significantly over the course of learning during hippocampal aSWRs (Figure 5A and B) (Wilcoxon rank sum test; p < 0.05)
evidence: Statistical test supports this with p < 0.05.

claim: In CA1, the reactivation strength remained constant from pre- to postlearning sessions.
source: In CA1, on the other hand, the reactivation strength remained constant from pre- to postlearning sessions (p = 0.337)
evidence: Statistical test shows no significant change with p = 0.337.

claim: The frequency of aSWR occurrences did not change between pre- and postlearning sessions.
source: The frequency of aSWR occurrences did not change between pre- and postlearning sessions (Pre n = 24, 0.08 Hz; Post n = 38, 0.09 Hz; Wilcoxon rank sum test; p = 0.2) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, C)
evidence: Statistical test shows no significant change with p = 0.2.

claim: During conditioning trials, aSWR rate decreased and was at its lowest during reward consumption.
source: During conditioning trials, aSWR rate decreased and was at its lowest during reward consumption (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: This is based on analysis of aSWR rates across trial periods.

claim: Average aSWR rates slightly increased from the beginning to the end of each session.
source: Average aSWR rates independent of task stage slightly increased from the beginning to the end of each session (n = 62; 0.06–0.1 Hz, Wilcoxon rank sum test; p < 0.01)
evidence: Statistical test supports this with p < 0.01.

claim: In CA1, assembly reactivation strength per aSWR increases gradually over the course of individual prelearning sessions for positively modulated assemblies.
source: We found that in CA1 assembly reactivation strength per aSWR increases gradually over the course of individual prelearning sessions for positively modulated assemblies (reactivation+) as well as for negatively modulated assemblies (reactivation−) during aSWRs (Figure 5C)
evidence: This is based on analysis of reactivation strength across trial blocks within sessions.

claim: In CA1, assembly reactivation strength per aSWR increases gradually over the course of individual prelearning sessions for negatively modulated assemblies.
source: We found that in CA1 assembly reactivation strength per aSWR increases gradually over the course of individual prelearning sessions for positively modulated assemblies (reactivation+) as well as for negatively modulated assemblies (reactivation−) during aSWRs (Figure 5C)
evidence: This is based on analysis of reactivation strength across trial blocks within sessions.

claim: In CA1, the within-session increase in reactivation was present in postlearning sessions for the reactivation+ assemblies.
source: This effect was also present in postlearning sessions for the reactivation+ assemblies (one-way ANOVA; CA1 pre+: p < 0.01, pre−: p < 0.05, post+: p < 0.001, post−: n.s.)
evidence: Statistical test supports this with p < 0.001 for post+ assemblies.

claim: In PFC, assembly reactivation strength slightly increased for positively modulated assemblies in postlearning sessions.
source: In PFC assembly reactivation strength slightly increased for positively modulated assemblies in postlearning sessions (Figure 5C)
evidence: This is based on analysis of reactivation strength across trial blocks within sessions.

claim: In CA1, the 25% most reactivated assemblies are suppressed during the trace and reward period after CS+ trials compared to CS− trials.
source: In CA1, we found that the 25 % most reactivated assemblies are suppressed during the trace and reward period after CS+ trials compared to CS− trials (Figure 5D) (Wilcoxon signed-rank; p < 0.001)
evidence: Statistical test supports this with p < 0.001.

claim: In PFC, the 25% most reactivated assemblies responded strongly during the reward period.
source: In PFC, on the other hand, the 25 % most reactivated assemblies responded strongly during the reward period (Figure 5E) (t-test, compared to pretrial baseline; p < 0.05)
evidence: Statistical test supports this with p < 0.05.

claim: In CA1, CS+ suppressed assemblies in both stimulus and trace periods were more reactivated during aSWRs compared to CS− suppressed assemblies and control, nonmodulated assemblies.
source: We found that, for CA1, CS+ suppressed assemblies in both stimulus and trace periods (i.e., assemblies that are more suppressed during CS+ trials than CS− trials) were more reactivated during aSWRs (Figure 6B) compared to CS− suppressed assemblies and control, nonmodulated assemblies
evidence: This is based on analysis of assembly reactivation strength grouped by trial-type modulation.

claim: In CA1, there is a negative correlation between the trial-type modulation score and the average aSWR reactivation of each assembly.
source: This effect was confirmed by the presence of a negative correlation between the trial-type modulation score and the average aSWR reactivation of each assembly (Figure 6C)
evidence: Correlation analysis supports this relationship.

claim: In CA1, CS− suppressed assemblies were also more strongly reactivated than control assemblies in prelearning sessions.
source: CS− suppressed assemblies were also more strongly reactivated than control assemblies in prelearning sessions (p < 0.05, Figure 6B)
evidence: Statistical test supports this with p < 0.05.

claim: In CS− trials, assemblies that were more suppressed during stimulus compared to trace period also reactivated more during aSWR.
source: and, in CS− trials, assemblies that were more suppressed during stimulus compared to trace period also reactivated more during aSWR (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is based on analysis of assembly reactivation strength grouped by trial-period modulation.

claim: In PFC, there was no preferential reactivation of CS+ or CS− specific assemblies.
source: In PFC, we did not observe preferential reactivation of CS+ or CS− specific assemblies (Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is based on analysis showing no differential reactivation by trial type.

claim: Coordinated reactivations of pairs of CA1 and PFC assemblies during aSWRs happens at chance levels.
source: We found that coordinated reactivations of pairs of CA1 and PFC assemblies during aSWRs happens at chance levels (Figure 6D)
evidence: This is based on analysis of co-occurrence of high reactivation in both areas.

claim: CA1 and PFC neurons undergo distinct learning-dependent changes at the single-cell level.
source: CA1 and PFC neurons undergo distinct learning-dependent changes at the single-cell level
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by multiple analyses of single-cell responses.

claim: CA1 and PFC maintain representations of cue identity at the population level.
source: and maintain representations of cue identity at the population level
evidence: This is supported by population vector analysis and classification results.

claim: Reactivation of task-related neuronal assemblies during hippocampal awake Sharp-Wave Ripples (aSWRs) changed within individual sessions in CA1.
source: In addition, reactivation of task-related neuronal assemblies during hippocampal awake Sharp-Wave Ripples (aSWRs) changed within individual sessions in CA1
evidence: This is supported by analysis of reactivation strength across trial blocks within sessions.

claim: Reactivation of task-related neuronal assemblies during hippocampal awake Sharp-Wave Ripples (aSWRs) changed over the course of multiple sessions in PFC.
source: and over the course of multiple sessions in PFC
evidence: This is supported by comparison of reactivation strength between pre- and postlearning sessions.

claim: There was no evidence for coordinated single cell activity during conditioning trials between CA1 and PFC.
source: Despite both areas being highly engaged and synchronized during the task, we found no evidence for coordinated single cell or assembly activity during conditioning trials or aSWR
evidence: This is based on reduced-rank regression analysis showing no task-specific changes in cross-area coordination.

claim: There was no evidence for coordinated assembly activity during aSWR between CA1 and PFC.
source: Despite both areas being highly engaged and synchronized during the task, we found no evidence for coordinated single cell or assembly activity during conditioning trials or aSWR
evidence: This is based on analysis showing chance-level co-occurrence of high reactivation.

claim: Persistent firing and reactivation of task-related neural activity patterns in CA1 and PFC support learning during classical conditioning.
source: Taken together, our findings support the notion that persistent firing and reactivation of task-related neural activity patterns in CA1 and PFC support learning during classical conditioning
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the overall findings.

claim: The ability to react to sensory cues with appropriate behavior is crucial for survival.
source: The ability to react to sensory cues with appropriate behavior is crucial for survival
evidence: This is a general statement based on established biological principles.

claim: Linking cues to actions likely requires the interplay between a large network of cortical and subcortical brain structures, including the medial prefrontal cortex (PFC) and the CA1 area of the hippocampus.
source: On the level of neuronal circuits, linking cues to actions likely requires the interplay between a large network of cortical and subcortical brain structures, including the medial prefrontal cortex (PFC) and the CA1 area of the hippocampus (Allen et al., 2017; Steinmetz et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Both CA1 and PFC have been found to respond to sensory cues and reward in various behavioral paradigms.
source: Both areas have been found to respond to sensory cues and reward in various behavioral paradigms (Aronov et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2013; Starkweather et al., 2018; Taxidis et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: CA1 and PFC are involved in action planning and execution.
source: and are involved in action planning and execution (Otis et al., 2017; Terada et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: PFC has been suggested to map contextual and sensory information to appropriate actions according to flexible rules.
source: PFC has been suggested to map contextual and sensory information to appropriate actions according to flexible rules (Euston and Gruber, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: PFC has been found to control the development and expression of anticipatory licking during sensory guided reward-seeking behavior.
source: Accordingly, PFC has been found to control the development and expression of anticipatory licking during sensory guided reward-seeking behavior (Otis et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: PFC maintains working memory representations of sensory cues over delay periods.
source: PFC also maintains working memory representations of sensory cues over delay periods (Funahashi et al., 1993; Goldman-Rakic, 1995)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CA1 responds to sensory cues and displays sustained activity during delay periods to support memory formation.
source: Similar to PFC, CA1 responds to sensory cues and displays sustained activity during delay periods to support memory formation (Hattori et al., 2015; McEchron et al., 1999; McEchron and Disterhoft, 1997)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: CA1 and PFC interact substantially during awake hippocampal Sharp-Wave Ripples (aSWRs).
source: Importantly, CA1 and PFC interact substantially during awake hippocampal Sharp-Wave Ripples (aSWRs) (Jadhav et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: aSWRs have been suggested to support planning of goal-directed actions in the context of spatial navigation.
source: aSWRs have been suggested to support planning of goal-directed actions in the context of spatial navigation (Ólafsdóttir et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The disruption of aSWRs leads to impairments in anticipatory behavior.
source: and the disruption of aSWRs leads to impairments in anticipatory behavior (Nokia et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Sensory cue representations are reactivated in hippocampal and corticohippocampal circuits during aSWRs.
source: In addition, sensory cue representations are reactivated in hippocampal and corticohippocampal circuits during aSWRs (Herzog et al., 2020; Rothschild et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Abundant Trace-Down like responses and sparse Trace-Up like responses have been described during aversive trace conditioning in CA1.
source: Similar to our study, abundant Trace-Down like responses and sparse Trace-Up like responses have been described during aversive trace conditioning in CA1 (Hattori et al., 2015; McEchron and Disterhoft, 1997)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The distinct pattern of mostly inhibition mixed with sparse excitation has been hypothesized to increase the signal-to-noise ratio to more efficiently propagate the signal of Trace-Up cells to downstream areas.
source: This distinct pattern of mostly inhibition mixed with sparse excitation has been hypothesized to increase the signal-to-noise ratio to more efficiently propagate the signal of Trace-Up cells to downstream areas (Hattori et al., 2015)
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous research cited in the text.

claim: Inhibition in CA1 might play an active role in suppressing well expected incoming stimuli, that is, reward delivery.
source: Inhibition in CA1 might, for example, play an active role in suppressing well expected incoming stimuli, that is, reward delivery (Bastos et al., 2012; Rummell et al., 2016; Stachenfeld et al., 2017)
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to related theoretical work.

claim: Higher numbers and stronger excitation of Trace-Up cells have been found in rat PFC and parts of rabbit PFC during aversive trace conditioning.
source: Specifically, higher numbers and stronger excitation of Trace-Up cells have also been found in rat PFC and parts of rabbit PFC during aversive trace conditioning (Hattori et al., 2014; Takehara-Nishiuchi and McNaughton, 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A learning-dependent reduction in responses to CS− like pseudoconditioning stimuli have been described in PFC.
source: A learning-dependent reduction in responses to CS− like pseudoconditioning stimuli have also previously been described in PFC (Hattori et al., 2014; Takehara-Nishiuchi and McNaughton, 2008; Weiss and Disterhoft, 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Sparse excitation with strong surrounding inhibition in CA1 and mostly excitation in PFC are two general coding principles employed to bridge the temporal gap between a salient cue and a behaviorally relevant event.
source: In combination, this suggests that sparse excitation with strong surrounding inhibition in CA1 and mostly excitation in PFC are two general coding principles employed to bridge the temporal gap between a salient cue and a behaviorally relevant event, independently of the appetitive or aversive nature of the event and the specific anticipatory action that it requires
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing current results with previous literature.

claim: Increased synchronization between CA1 and PFC during spatial working memory tasks have previously been reported predominantly in the theta frequency (4–12 Hz).
source: Increased synchronization between both areas during spatial working memory tasks have previously been reported predominantly in the theta frequency (4–12 Hz) (Battaglia et al., 2011; Benchenane et al., 2010; Jones and Wilson, 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: During trace-conditioning mice were mostly stationary and did not display strong hippocampal theta oscillations.
source: However, during trace-conditioning mice were mostly stationary and did not display strong hippocampal theta oscillations
evidence: This is an observation from the current study.

claim: High-frequency coherence during trace conditioning likely results from a different underlying mechanism than theta synchronization during spatial tasks.
source: and high-frequency coherence therefore likely results from a different underlying mechanism
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of theta oscillations.

claim: CA1 and PFC either process conditioning trials in parallel rather than in series or rely on intermediate structures for effective communication.
source: CA1 and PFC therefore either process conditioning trials in parallel rather than in series or rely on intermediate structures (e.g., entorhinal cortex) for effective communication (Insel and Takehara-Nishiuchi, 2013)
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the lack of single-cell coordination, with a citation to support the role of intermediate structures.

claim: Earlier reports found coordinated aSWR reactivation of behavioral sequences during learning of spatial memory tasks in CA1 and PFC.
source: Earlier reports found coordinated aSWR reactivation of behavioral sequences during learning of spatial memory tasks in CA1 and PFC, respectively (Kaefer et al., 2020; Shin et al., 2019; Shin and Jadhav, 2016; Tang et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Close loop disruption of aSWRs has been shown to impair performance in spatial memory task and slow learning during conditioning.
source: In addition, close loop disruption of aSWRs has been shown to impair performance in spatial memory task and slow learning during conditioning
evidence: This is a statement about previous research findings.

claim: Physiological evidence for reactivation of neural assembly patterns during aSWRs in a nonspatial task in either CA1 or PFC had been missing.
source: However, physiological evidence for reactivation of neural assembly patterns during aSWRs in a nonspatial task in either CA1 or PFC had been missing (Joo and Frank, 2018; Ólafsdóttir et al., 2018)
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature with citations.

claim: The current data provide the missing link for physiological evidence of reactivation during aSWRs in a nonspatial task.
source: Our data now provide this missing link
evidence: This is a claim about the contribution of the current study.

claim: Both CA1 and PFC support learning on different timescales and levels of complexity, with the hippocampus adapting fast to detailed new experiences and the PFC adapting more slowly to behaviorally important variables that remain stable over time.
source: This is well in line with the idea that both areas support learning on different timescales and levels of complexity, with the hippocampus adapting fast to detailed new experiences and the PFC adapting more slowly to behaviorally important variables that remain stable over time (McClelland et al., 1995; Takehara-Nishiuchi and McNaughton, 2008; Takehara et al., 2003)
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of established theories, supported by citations.

claim: Preferential reactivation of CS suppressed assemblies during aSWR provides additional evidence that suppression in CA1 during CS+ trials plays a pivotal role during trace conditioning.
source: This preferential reactivation of CS suppressed assemblies during aSWR, provides additional evidence that suppression in CA1 during CS+ trials plays a pivotal role during trace conditioning and might be relevant to actively encode stimulus identity or to predict upcoming task events
evidence: This is an interpretation of the reactivation findings.
